page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E4.Flex.32-512 is a high-memory compute instance powered by the AMD EPYC 7J13 processor built on the x86_64 architecture. Operating at a base frequency of 2.55 GHz, this virtual machine is provisioned with 32 dedicated physical cores and 64 vCPUs leveraging two threads per core. The host supplies 512.0 GB of system memory, establishing a 1:8 vCPU-to-memory allocation of 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU.

This server instance contains no local solid-state storage or bundled NVMe drives, requiring workloads to rely exclusively on remote block storage for persistent filesystems and data storage. Hardware acceleration is not present, as the instance features zero GPUs. Network ingress and egress are supported by one included complimentary public IPv4 address.

The dense memory ratio relative to core count delivers efficient resource utilization for setups where RAM footprint dictates scaling thresholds. By omitting costly hardware accelerators and dedicated local disks, the instance provides qualitative cost efficiency for memory-heavy platforms. Primary workload fits include large in-memory databases, distributed caching layers, enterprise application servers, and big data batch processing pipelines.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E4.Flex.32-512 is an x86_64 compute instance configured with 32 dedicated physical cores and 64 virtual CPUs based on the AMD EPYC 7J13 processor running at a base clock speed of 2.55 GHz. The system provides 512.0 GB of system memory, yielding an elevated 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 8.0 GB of memory per virtual thread. There are no discrete hardware accelerators or local NVMe storage drives bundled with this shape, necessitating reliance on remote network-attached block storage for persistent operational data. One complimentary public IPv4 address is provisioned alongside the compute resources. The balanced hardware ratio positions this configuration efficiently for memory-demanding enterprise deployments, including large in-memory key-value databases, comprehensive enterprise resource planning platforms, caching layers, and high-throughput data processing pipelines requiring substantial memory residency without the overhead of physical accelerator hardware.
